note: soirée is the evening as a stretch of time, so this is a goodbye wish; bonsoir is the greeting. Also 'a party': 'une soirée chez Paul'.

example.en: Goodbye and have a nice evening!

note: bon + soir. Said from roughly 6 pm, both on arriving and on leaving. 'Bonne soirée' is the wish 'have a nice evening'.
Both hello and goodbye between friends and young people; never to a shopkeeper or a stranger. From Latin salus 'health, safety', the root of English 'salute'.
For someone you will see again the same day. Pronounced 'a too-ta-leur' with the t of tout linking to à. Often shortened to 'à tout'.
Only said when someone is going to bed. For leaving a party in the evening use 'bonne soirée'.
Playful hello among friends, family and in text messages; also the cuckoo's call and 'peekaboo'. Never for formal settings.
The tu version, for friends, family and children. Written STP in text messages.
Always plural, like English. From féliciter, Latin felix 'happy, lucky'. 'Toutes mes félicitations!' = my warmest congratulations.
beaucoup is literally beau + coup, 'a fine stroke'. The final p is silent. Stronger still: 'merci mille fois' (a thousand times).
A warm way to accept an offer or to reply to merci, especially in the south of France. 'Volontiers' (willingly) is another.
The polite reply to merci, and also 'please, go ahead' when holding a door. With tu: 'je t'en prie'.
Imperative of excuser + moi, joined by a hyphen. Used to get attention or to apologise lightly. The final z is silent. With tu: excuse-moi.

example.en: Excuse me, where is the station?

note: English 'pardon' is this French word. Said after bumping into someone, and with rising intonation ('Pardon ?') to ask someone to repeat.
From Latin desolare 'to leave alone'. A woman writes désolée; the extra e is silent, so both forms sound the same. 'Je suis désolé(e)' is the full apology.
Short for 'enchanté de faire votre connaissance'. Agrees with the speaker: a woman says enchantée.

example.en: Pleased to meet you, my name is Claire.

note: French asks how you 'go'. The normally silent t of comment is pronounced here in liaison with allez. The standard answer: 'Je vais bien, merci.'
chance means luck, not chance: 'avoir de la chance' = to be lucky. Actors say 'merde' instead, as in English 'break a leg'.
From Old French oïl, which gave the name 'langue d'oïl' to northern French. Informal 'ouais' = yeah. After a negative question say 'si', not oui.
The n is nasal: the lips do not close. 'Non merci' refuses politely; inside a sentence negation needs ne ... pas.
As a greeting it is always the feminine form bienvenue (short for 'la bienvenue'). 'Bienvenue en France!'
bientôt = bien + tôt 'well early'. The circumflex on tôt marks the s of the old spelling tost. Same pattern: à plus tard (see you later).
demain comes from Latin de mane 'from the morning'. The pattern 'à + time' works for any goodbye: à lundi, à ce soir.
journée is a day as a stretch of time, so this is a goodbye wish, never a hello. Shopkeepers say it as you leave; the reply is 'merci, vous aussi'.
mon + sieur, an old form of seigneur. Pronounced roughly 'meu-syeu': neither the n of mon nor the final r is heard. Plural messieurs; abbreviation M.
ma + dame (Latin domina). Plural mesdames, abbreviation Mme. 'Mademoiselle' for unmarried women was dropped from French official forms in 2012.

example.en: Good morning madam, good morning sir.

note: From Italian zero, ultimately Arabic sifr 'empty', which also gave French chiffre (digit). Temperature: 'il fait zéro'.
Also the indefinite article 'a'. The masculine n is nasal; the feminine une has a clear n sound. 'Vingt et un', 'trente et un' use 'et' only for 21-71.

example.target: Un café et une bière, s'il vous plaît.
example.en: One coffee and one beer, please.

note: The x is silent, but before a vowel it sounds as z: deux heures 'deu-zeur'. Latin duo.
Final s silent except in liaison: trois ans 'trwa-zan'. Latin tres.
qu = k, final e silent: 'katr'. Latin quattuor. 'quatre-quarts' is a pound cake made of four equal parts.
The final q is pronounced as k ('sank'), though it is often dropped before a consonant: cinq minutes 'sin minut'. Latin quinque.
Three pronunciations: 'sees' alone, 'see' before a consonant (six livres), 'seez' before a vowel (six ans).
The p is silent, the t is pronounced: 'set'. Latin septem.
The h blocks liaison and elision ('le huit mai'). The t is heard alone and before a vowel (huit ans) but drops before a consonant (huit jours).
Final f is pronounced, and turns into v before ans and heures: neuf heures 'neu-veur'. Latin novem. neuf also means 'new'.
Behaves like six: 'dees', 'dee' before a consonant, 'deez' before a vowel. 17-19 are built on it: dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf.
Latin undecim. Like huit it refuses liaison and elision: 'le onze novembre'.
Latin duodecim. 'une douzaine' = a dozen, and 'une douzaine de' is used loosely for 'about twelve'.
Latin quindecim. 'quinze jours' (fifteen days) is the usual way to say a fortnight / two weeks.
g and t silent: 'vin', a homophone of vin (wine). The t reappears in 21-29: vingt-deux 'vint-deu'. 21 is vingt et un.
Latin triginta. 31 = trente et un, then trente-deux; the same pattern runs through quarante (40), cinquante (50).
The x is pronounced as s: 'swa-sant'. Latin sexaginta.
French keeps counting on from sixty: 71 soixante et onze, 72 soixante-douze ... 79 soixante-dix-neuf. Belgium and Switzerland say septante.
A relic of counting in twenties (compare English 'four score'). The final s is dropped when another number follows: quatre-vingt-un. Swiss French says huitante.
91 is quatre-vingt-onze, 99 quatre-vingt-dix-neuf. Belgium and Switzerland use nonante.
Latin centum. 'deux cents' takes an s unless another number follows (deux cent un). The t is silent except in liaison: cent ans 'san-tan'.
Invariable: deux mille, never with s. Pronounced 'meel'. Years are read the same way: deux mille vingt-six.
Written 1er / 1re. The only ordinal used in dates: 'le premier mai', but 'le deux mai'. From Latin primarius.
Ordinals add -ième to the number: troisième, dixième, vingtième. 'second/seconde' is an older alternative, traditionally when there are only two. Written 2e.
Before a noun it is invariable and hyphenated: une demi-heure; after, it agrees: une heure et demie. 'Un demi' in a bar is a 25 cl glass of beer.
Latin familia. The -ille ending sounds like 'ee-y': 'fa-mee-y'. 'en famille' = with the family.
Latin mater. Three homophones: mère (mother), mer (sea), maire (mayor). Informal: maman.
Latin pater. Informal: papa. 'le père Noël' = Father Christmas.
Watch out: parents also means 'relatives' in general (des parents éloignés = distant relatives). The final s and the t are silent.
Latin frater. English 'friar' is this word, borrowed from Old French. 'le petit frère' = little brother.
The ligature œ is called 'e dans l'o'. Latin soror. Pronounced 'seur', final r heard.
Odd spelling: the l is silent but the final s is pronounced, 'feess'. Latin filius. Plural is spelled the same: les fils.
Both 'daughter' and 'girl', with -ille sounding 'ee-y'. 'jeune fille' = young girl; 'petite fille' = little girl, but 'petite-fille' = granddaughter.
Same form for both sexes; only the article changes. From Latin infans 'not speaking', the source of English 'infant'. Plural les enfants with a z liaison.
A borrowing from English 'baby' in the 18th-19th century, respelled with French accents. Used for girls too: 'le bébé' stays masculine.
Informal: papi or papy. Plural grands-pères.
grand has no -e even though mère is feminine: a relic of Old French, where grand had one form for both genders. Informal: mamie.

example.target: Nous allons chez nos grands-parents dimanche.
example.en: We are going to our grandparents' on Sunday.

note: Latin maritus. The verb is se marier (to get married), and a wedding is un mariage, with one r.
Both 'woman' and 'wife'. Irregular pronunciation: 'fam', the e sounding like a. Latin femina; English 'female' and 'feminine' share the root.
From Latin companio 'one who shares bread (panis)', like 'companion'. Casual friend, but 'mon copain / ma copine' with a possessive usually means boyfriend / girlfriend.
Silent h (h muet), so the article elides: l'homme, and 'les hommes' has a z liaison. Latin homo 'human being'; the pronoun 'on' (one, we) comes from the same word.
Also the traditional, now rather dated, word for a waiter. Probably of Frankish origin; the ç keeps the c soft before o.
Latin avunculus (mother's brother). English 'uncle' was borrowed from this French word.
Old French ante (Latin amita) gave English 'aunt'; French later grew an initial t, perhaps from children's 't'ante'.
The masculine ends in a nasal vowel ('cou-zan'); the feminine adds -e and the n is heard ('cou-zeen').
Always plural; the s is silent, 'jan'. For one person use 'une personne'. 'les jeunes gens' = young people.
Always feminine, even for a man: 'il est une personne gentille'. With ne it means 'nobody': 'Je ne vois personne.'
Latin vicinus. 'le voisinage' = the neighbourhood.
Reflexive -er verb. The l doubles where the ending is silent (je m'appelle) but not in nous/vous forms (nous nous appelons).

example.en: My name is Thomas. And you?

note: Latin panis. Nasal ending: 'pan' with no n sound. The bakery is 'la boulangerie'; a baguette is bought 'une baguette, s'il vous plaît'.
Four letters, one sound: 'o'. From Latin aqua. Plural les eaux. In a restaurant ask for 'une carafe d'eau' (tap water) or 'de l'eau gazeuse' (sparkling).
Latin vinum. Homophone of vingt (twenty). 'du vin rouge / blanc / rosé'; 'la carte des vins' = the wine list.
Borrowed in the Middle Ages from Dutch bier, replacing the older Gaulish-derived cervoise. 'une pression' = a draught beer.
Latin lac, lactis. Final t silent: 'lè'. 'un café au lait', 'un chocolat au lait'.
From Latin formaticus (caseus), 'cheese made in a form (mould)': formage became fromage by swapping the r. France counts well over a thousand kinds.
Via Italian caffè from Turkish kahve, Arabic qahwa. 'un café' ordered in France is a small espresso; a 'café crème' comes with milk. Also means the café itself.
From the Min Chinese word te, which reached Europe through Dutch traders; the h is purely decorative. 'un thé au citron', 'un thé nature' (plain).
Arabic sukkar via Italian zucchero; English 'sugar' came through Old French. 'un sucre' = a sugar lump.
Latin sal. 'Passe-moi le sel.' The adjective is salé (salty), and 'le gros sel' is coarse sea salt.
Latin butyrum, from Greek, the same root as English 'butter'. 'un croissant au beurre'; 'beurre demi-sel' is lightly salted Breton butter.

example.target: Du pain et du beurre, c'est simple et bon.
example.en: Bread and butter, simple and good.

note: Singular 'euf' with the f sounded; in the plural les œufs both f and s go silent: 'lé zeu'. Latin ovum.
Originally 'food' in general (Latin vivenda, 'things to live on'), later narrowed to meat. 'Je ne mange pas de viande' = I don't eat meat.
Diminutive of poule (hen). Final t silent. In slang un poulet is also a police officer.
Latin piscis. Mind the spelling: double ss = s sound; single s, as in poison, = z sound.

example.target: Le poisson du jour est très frais.
example.en: The fish of the day is very fresh.

note: Latin pomum meant any fruit; French narrowed it to the apple. 'une pomme' is also a potato in compounds (pommes frites).
Same image as Dutch aardappel. In speech 'une patate' is the casual word, and 'frites' are 'pommes frites'.
False friend: légume means any vegetable, not only beans and peas. Latin legumen.
The circumflex marks a lost s: Old French gastel. Plural gâteaux. 'c'est du gâteau' = it's a piece of cake (easy).
déjeuner is literally 'to break the fast' (dé- + jeûner). Typically bread or croissant with coffee; a cooked breakfast is rare.
In Belgium, Switzerland and Quebec déjeuner means breakfast, dîner lunch and souper dinner. The verb is the same word: 'on déjeune à midi'.
The circumflex replaces the s of Old French disner, from which English 'dinner' was borrowed. Also a verb: 'nous dînons à huit heures'.
Regular -er verb; nous mangeons keeps an e so the g stays soft. Latin manducare 'to chew'.
Irregular: the stem changes to buv- in nous/vous. Past participle bu ('j'ai bu'). From Latin bibere.
Regular -er verb from 'la cuisine', which means both the kitchen and cooking; English borrowed 'cuisine' back for the cooking style.
Originally an 18th-century Paris 'restoring' broth; the establishments that served it took the name and the word travelled the world. Final t silent.
From servir. To call one, say 'S'il vous plaît!' rather than the dated 'Garçon!'. Serveur also means a computer server.
The menu you read from is la carte; ordering 'à la carte' means dish by dish. The same word means map and card.
False friend: in a French restaurant le menu is a fixed-price meal of two or three courses, often 'le menu du jour'. Ask for la carte to see everything.

example.target: Je prends le menu à vingt euros.
example.en: I'll have the twenty-euro set menu.

note: The waiter adds up what you had. You usually have to ask for it: 'L'addition, s'il vous plaît.' In a café 'la note' is also heard.
Latin tabula. Final e silent: 'tabl'. 'une table pour deux' = a table for two; 'à table!' = dinner's ready!
Both the material and the drinking glass. Homophones: vert (green), vers (towards), ver (worm). 'un verre de vin', 'prendre un verre' = to have a drink.
Late Latin butticula; English 'bottle' came through Old French. -eille sounds like 'ay' ('bou-tay').
From asseoir 'to seat': first the diner's place at table, then the plate. 'ne pas être dans son assiette' = to feel out of sorts.
Diminutive of fourche (pitchfork). Forks reached French tables only in the 16th century.
Latin cultellus. Plural couteaux. 'un coup de couteau' = a stab.
Also spelled cuiller. From Latin cochlearium, a small spoon for eating snails (cochlea). 'une cuillère à café' = teaspoon.
'le plat du jour' = today's special; 'le plat principal' = main course. As an adjective plat means flat: 'de l'eau plate' = still water.
False friend for Americans: in France l'entrée is the first course, the 'entry' into the meal, not the main dish.

example.target: En entrée, je voudrais une soupe.
example.en: As a starter I'd like a soup.

note: From desservir 'to clear the table': what is served once the table is cleared. Double s = s sound; 'le désert' with one s is the desert.
pour + boire: money 'for a drink'. Service is included by law in France ('service compris'), so a tip is a small optional extra.
Regular -er verb. Means 'to order' food or goods as well as 'to command'. 'Vous avez choisi ?' is what the waiter asks.
Regular -er verb. 'une réservation au nom de...' = a booking in the name of...
Conditional of vouloir: the polite way to order or ask. 'Je veux' (I want) sounds blunt to French ears.

example.target: Je voudrais un verre de vin rouge.
example.en: I would like a glass of red wine.

note: Said to anyone about to eat, including strangers at the next table. Final t silent.
Short for 'à votre santé' (to your health). Also 'tchin-tchin'. Custom says you look people in the eye as you clink glasses.
Masculine -eux is silent at the end; feminine -euse adds a z sound. 'C'était délicieux' pleases any host.
Sitting 'en terrasse' at a café is a French institution; prices can be higher there than at the bar (au comptoir).
Tap water, served free on request with a meal. If you don't say carafe, you may get bottled water and a bill for it.

example.target: Une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît.
example.en: A jug of tap water, please.

note: From croître 'to grow': the crescent moon is 'la lune croissante'. The pastry is a Vienna-inspired 'viennoiserie', not a French invention.

example.target: Deux croissants et un pain au chocolat.
example.en: Two croissants and one pain au chocolat.

note: From Latin viaticum 'provisions for the road'. English 'voyage' is the same word, narrowed to sea journeys. 'Bon voyage!' = have a good trip.
Regular -er verb; nous voyageons keeps the e after g. 'un voyageur / une voyageuse' = a traveller.
Only for trains; a bus station is 'la gare routière', a metro station 'la station'. 'Gare!' as an exclamation means 'watch out!'.
aéro- + port. Paris's airports: Charles-de-Gaulle (Roissy) and Orly. Final t silent.
Train, plane and show tickets are billets; a bus or metro ticket is 'un ticket'. Billet also means a banknote. Final t silent: 'bee-yè'.

example.target: Un billet pour Marseille, s'il vous plaît.

note: passe + port: a pass for leaving by a port or gate. The s is pronounced, the final t is silent: 'pass-por'.
'faire sa valise' = to pack. Luggage in general is 'les bagages' (always plural in French).
The circumflex marks the s of Old French hostel, which English kept in 'hostel' and 'hotel'. 'l'hôtel de ville' is the town hall, not a hotel.

example.target: J'ai une réservation au nom de Martin.
example.en: I have a booking in the name of Martin.

note: A town map is un plan; a road or country map is une carte. 'le plan du métro' = the metro map.
gauche also means 'clumsy', the sense English borrowed. 'Tournez à gauche' = turn left; 'sur votre gauche' = on your left.
droit = straight, right, law. 'à droite' is right as a direction; 'tout droit' is straight ahead.

example.target: La banque est à droite, après le pont.
example.en: The bank is on the right, after the bridge.

note: Don't confuse with 'à droite' (right). Pronounced 'too drwa': the t of tout is silent before a consonant. 'Continuez tout droit' = keep going straight on.
'C'est loin ?' = is it far? 'loin de' = far from; 'au loin' = in the distance. Latin longe.
près de la gare = near the station. Without de: 'c'est tout près' = it's very close. The s is silent.
The four compass points are Germanic loans (Old English via Norman): nord, sud, est, ouest. Final d silent. 'le Nord' is also a département.
Unlike nord, the final d of sud is pronounced. 'le Sud' = the South of France; 'le Midi' is the traditional name for it.
Pronounced 'est' with the t heard, unlike the verb form est (is), which is 'è'.
Pronounced 'west', with the final t heard. 'la côte ouest' = the west coast.
Celtic (Gaulish) origin. 'le chemin de fer' = railway, literally 'iron road'. 'Je cherche mon chemin' = I'm trying to find my way.
Past participle of perdre (to lose). 'Je suis perdu(e)' = I'm lost. 'objets perdus' = lost property.
Irregular -ir verb that drops the t in the singular. Uses être in the past: 'je suis parti(e)'. 'à partir de' = from (a time).
Regular -er, with être in the past: 'nous sommes arrivés'. Also 'to happen': 'Qu'est-ce qui arrive ?'. From Latin ad ripam 'to the shore'.

example.target: Le train arrive à dix heures.

note: Regular -er verb. 'Tournez à gauche au feu' = turn left at the traffic light. Also 'to shoot' a film.
From voler, which means both 'to fly' and 'to steal'; so un vol is also a theft. Context decides. 'le vol Paris-Nice'.
Originally any vehicle (Latin vectura 'transport'); a carriage is still 'une voiture' on a train. 'en voiture' = by car.

example.target: On y va en voiture ou en train ?
example.en: Shall we go by car or by train?

note: From traîner 'to drag'; English 'train' borrowed it. The TGV (train à grande vitesse) is the high-speed train. 'en train de' = in the middle of doing.
Coined by the aviation pioneer Clément Ader from Latin avis 'bird'. 'en avion' = by plane; 'par avion' = airmail.
Short for autobus. The final s is pronounced: 'buss'. A coach for long distances is 'un car' (short for autocar).
Short for 'chemin de fer métropolitain', the Paris system opened in 1900. 'métro, boulot, dodo' = the daily grind (metro, work, sleep).
Short for vélocipède ('swift-foot'). The formal word is 'la bicyclette'. 'faire du vélo' = to cycle.

example.target: Je vais au travail à vélo.
example.en: I go to work by bike.

note: Short for taximètre, the fare meter. Final i: 'tak-see'. 'une station de taxis' = a taxi rank.
Borrowed from Old English bat (boat) via Norman French. Plural bateaux. 'en bateau' = by boat.
Short for motocyclette. 'à moto' = by motorbike. Feminine despite ending in -o.
'un camionneur' = a lorry driver; 'une camionnette' = a van.
Borrowed from English in the 19th century, now usually shortened to 'le tram'. Many French cities rebuilt tram networks after 1985.
Metro stop, taxi rank or petrol station ('station-service'); a railway station is 'la gare'. Pronounced 'sta-syon'.
From arrêter, to stop. 'l'arrêt de bus'. The circumflex marks the lost s of 'arrest', which English kept.
Also a riverside embankment, as in the Paris 'quais de Seine'. English 'quay' is the same Celtic-rooted word. Pronounced 'kè'.

example.target: Le train part du quai numéro trois.
example.en: The train leaves from platform three.

note: -teur / -trice pair, like acteur / actrice. A taxi driver is 'un chauffeur de taxi', a word English borrowed.
Shortened to 'le permis': 'passer son permis' = to take one's driving test. Driving age is 18 in France.
From Latin essentia; English 'essence' is the same word. Diesel is 'le gazole'. 'faire le plein' = to fill up.
Irregular -re verb with -s- in the plural; past participle conduit. From Latin conducere 'to lead together'. Also 'to lead someone' somewhere.
Irregular: single n in nous/vous, double n in ils prennent. Used for transport: 'prendre le bus'. Past participle pris.

example.target: Je prends le métro tous les jours.
example.en: I take the metro every day.

en: to get on, to go up
note: Regular -er verb; with être in the past when no object follows ('je suis monté'). 'monter dans le train' = to get on the train.

en: to get off, to go down
note: Regular -re verb. 'Vous descendez à la prochaine ?' is what you ask in a crowded metro. Takes être in the past.
False friend: it means to wait, not to attend. No preposition: 'j'attends le bus'. Regular -re verb.

example.target: Nous attendons le bus depuis vingt minutes.
example.en: We have been waiting for the bus for twenty minutes.

note: From Latin rupta (via) 'broken-through way'. English 'route' is the same word. 'en route!' = let's go; 'la route nationale' is a main road.
auto + route. Most French motorways are toll roads: 'le péage' = toll.
'Je suis en retard' = I'm late. For 'late' as an hour of the day say 'tard': 'il est tard'. Retard is a plain word in French, not an insult.
Silent h, so the article elides. Latin hora. 'Il est trois heures' = it's three o'clock. 'à l'heure' = on time; 'de bonne heure' = early.
The t of est links to il: 'è-teel'. Answer: 'Il est deux heures et demie' (half past two) or 'midi' (noon). France uses the 24-hour clock in writing.

example.target: Quelle heure est-il ? — Il est midi.
example.en: What time is it? — It's noon.

note: Latin diurnum. 'jour' is the unit (trois jours); 'la journée' is the day as it is lived (une belle journée). 'tous les jours' = every day.
Latin septimana 'seven-fold'. 'la semaine prochaine' = next week; 'en semaine' = on weekdays.
Latin mensis. The s is silent and the plural is spelled the same: 'trois mois'. Homophone of moi (me).
Two words for year: 'un an' counts (j'ai vingt ans) while 'une année' describes (une bonne année). 'Bonne année!' = Happy New Year.

literal: on the day of this day
note: au jour d'hui, where hui came from Latin hodie 'today'. The word doubles 'day' twice; 'au jour d'aujourd'hui' triples it and is common but mocked.
Latin de mane 'from the morning'. 'après-demain' = the day after tomorrow; 'demain matin' = tomorrow morning.
Latin heri. Pronounced 'yèr' with the r heard. 'avant-hier' = the day before yesterday; 'hier soir' = last night.
From 'main tenant', 'holding in hand', i.e. at this very moment. 'à partir de maintenant' = from now on.
'ce matin' = this morning; 'du matin' = a.m.: 'huit heures du matin'. The longer 'la matinée' is the morning as a stretch of time.
après + midi (noon). Can be masculine or feminine; dictionaries now prefer masculine. 'cet après-midi' = this afternoon.
'ce soir' = tonight (this evening); 'du soir' = p.m. for evening hours: 'sept heures du soir'. Bonsoir and bonne soirée come from it.
Latin nox, noctis. Final t silent: 'nwee'. 'cette nuit' = tonight (late) or last night; 'la nuit' = at night.
'Moon's day', Latin lunae dies: days of the week are not capitalised in French. 'le lundi' = on Mondays; 'lundi' alone = this coming Monday.

example.target: Le musée est fermé le lundi.
example.en: The museum is closed on Mondays.

note: Latin Martis dies, the day of Mars, like English 'Tuesday' is Tiw's day. 'Mardi gras' = Shrove Tuesday, 'fat Tuesday'.
Latin Mercurii dies. French schoolchildren traditionally had Wednesday afternoon free.
Latin Jovis dies, the day of Jove, matching English 'Thursday' (Thor's day).
Latin Veneris dies; English Friday honours the goddess Frigg instead. 'vendredi soir' = Friday evening.
From Latin sabbati dies, the Sabbath, unlike English 'Saturday' (Saturn's day).
From Latin dies dominicus. The French week starts on Monday, so dimanche is the last day on calendars. 'un dimanche' = a lazy Sunday.

example.target: Dimanche, on déjeune chez mes parents.
example.en: On Sunday we're having lunch at my parents'.

note: Latin Januarius, after the two-faced god Janus. Months are not capitalised: 'en janvier', 'le 15 janvier'.
From Latin Augustus. Usually pronounced simply 'oo' ('ou'), sometimes 'oot'; the a and the circumflex are silent. France largely goes on holiday in août.
Latin december, 'tenth month' of the old Roman year. 'le 25 décembre' = Christmas Day, 'Noël'.
Borrowed from English with a French hyphen. 'Bon week-end!' Quebec prefers 'la fin de semaine'.
Latin rubeus. Same form for both genders. 'le vin rouge', 'rouge à lèvres' = lipstick, 'le Moulin Rouge'.
A Frankish word (compare English 'blue'), not Latin. Plural bleus (irregular for -eu). 'les Bleus' = the French national teams.
Latin viridis. Masculine vert sounds like verre (glass) and vers; the feminine verte sounds the t. 'le feu vert' = green light.
Same form m/f. 'le maillot jaune' is the Tour de France leader's jersey; 'les Gilets jaunes' the 2018 protest movement.
Latin niger. 'un café noir' = black coffee; 'le film noir' and 'la bête noire' passed into English.
Frankish blank, the same root as English 'blank'. The c is silent in blanc but becomes 'sh' in blanche. 'le vin blanc', 'Mont Blanc'.
Frankish origin, like English 'grey'. Silent s in gris, z sound in grise. 'la grisaille' = dreary grey weather.
Same word as the flower, la rose. Invariable for gender; 'voir la vie en rose' = to see life through rose-tinted glasses.
Named after the fruit, and invariable: 'des chaussures orange'. The fruit came through Arabic and Spanish from Sanskrit.
From the flower, la violette. The t is silent in violet and pronounced in violette. 'violet' covers both purple and violet.
Literally 'chestnut', and invariable: 'des yeux marron'. For hair, say brun / brune or châtain instead.
Latin color. 'De quelle couleur est... ?' = what colour is...? English 'colour' kept the French -our ending.

example.target: De quelle couleur est ta voiture ?

note: 'bleu clair' = light blue; colour compounds are invariable: 'des yeux bleu clair'. Also 'clear': 'c'est clair' = that's clear.
'vert foncé' = dark green. For 'dark' as in 'it's dark outside' use 'il fait noir' or 'sombre'.
Latin circulus. 'un cercle vicieux'. The adjective is rond; the Paris ring road is 'le périphérique'.
From Latin quadratus. Also an adjective: 'un mètre carré' = a square metre. A town square is 'une place', not a carré.
Pronounced 'tree-angl'. The instrument and the shape. 'un triangle amoureux' = a love triangle.
Latin rectus 'right' + angulus: a right-angled shape. Adjective: rectangulaire.
Latin rotundus. 'un rond-point' = a roundabout; 'une table ronde' = a round table. The d is silent in rond, heard in ronde.
Latin linea. A metro line is 'la ligne 1'; 'en ligne' = online; 'garder la ligne' = to keep one's figure.
Also a full stop and a score point. 'Le point' is the dot; 'la pointe' is a sharp tip. Nasal ending: 'pwan'.
'en forme de cœur' = heart-shaped. 'être en forme' = to be fit / in good shape.
Latin crux. Final x silent: 'krwa'. 'la Croix-Rouge' = the Red Cross; 'faire une croix sur' = to give up on something.
Possibly of Germanic origin; English 'blonde' kept the French feminine. 'une bière blonde' = a lager.
Germanic root shared with English 'brown'. Used for hair and skin, and for beer ('une brune'); for objects use marron.

example.target: Elle est brune et son frère est blond.
example.en: She is dark-haired and her brother is blond.

note: Latin corpus. Both p and s are silent: 'kor'. 'le corps humain'. English 'corpse' and 'corps' come from it.
The circumflex marks the s of Old French teste, from Latin testa 'pot', a slang word for head that replaced caput. 'J'ai mal à la tête.'
Plural of cheveu, from Latin capillus; always plural for the hair on your head. 'les poils' is body hair. 'se couper les cheveux' = to get a haircut.
One of the most irregular plurals: un œil, deux yeux ('yeu', with a z liaison: 'dé-zyeu'). 'un coup d'œil' = a glance.
Latin nasus. The z is silent: 'né'. Plural is spelled the same. 'avoir du nez' = to have good instincts.
Latin bucca 'cheek'. 'le bouche-à-oreille' = word of mouth; 'une bouche de métro' = a metro entrance.
Latin dens, dentis; 'dentist' is the same root. Final t silent: 'dan'. 'se brosser les dents' = to brush one's teeth.
Latin auricula. -eille sounds 'ay': 'o-ray'. 'une boucle d'oreille' = an earring.
Latin manus. Feminine despite the missing -e. 'serrer la main' = to shake hands; 'fait main' = handmade.

example.target: Lave-toi les mains avant de manger.

note: Latin bracchium. Final s silent: 'bra'. 'bras dessus, bras dessous' = arm in arm.
From Late Latin gamba 'hoof, leg', which also gave English 'gammon' and 'jamb'. 'à toutes jambes' = at full speed.
Latin pes, pedis. Final d silent: 'pyé'. 'à pied' = on foot; 'un coup de pied' = a kick.
Latin dorsum. Final s silent: 'do'. 'J'ai mal au dos' = my back hurts; 'le dossier' (file) comes from the back of a chair.
Latin venter. 'J'ai mal au ventre' = I have a stomach ache. 'l'estomac' is the organ.
Latin cor, cordis; the œ ligature is pronounced 'eu'. 'par cœur' = by heart; 'avoir mal au cœur' means to feel sick, not heartache.
Latin sanitas. 'en bonne santé' = healthy. As a toast, 'Santé!'. 'la Sécurité sociale' pays for most health care.
Same form m/f; mal + Latin habitus 'badly kept'. 'tomber malade' = to fall ill. 'un malade' = a patient.

example.target: Il est malade depuis trois jours.
example.en: He has been ill for three days.

note: Formally one word for both sexes ('le médecin' even for a woman; 'la médecin' is now also used). Pronounced 'méd-san'. 'chez le médecin' = at the doctor's.
The circumflex replaces the s of Old French hospital, which English kept. Plural hôpitaux. 'les urgences' = A&E / the ER.
Recognisable by the green cross outside. French pharmacies sell medicine only; cosmetics and toiletries also, but no groceries. ph = f.
False friend: 'la médecine' is the science; the pills are 'les médicaments'. 'sur ordonnance' = on prescription.
'J'ai mal à la gorge / au dos / aux pieds.' The body part takes à + article. 'Ça fait mal' = it hurts.
From Greek rheuma 'flow' via Latin, hence the h. 'J'ai un rhume' or 'je suis enrhumé(e)' = I have a cold. 'le rhume des foins' = hay fever.
Irregular -ir verb that drops the m in the singular. Latin dormire. 'dormir comme un bébé'; 'faire dodo' is baby talk for sleeping.
Reflexive for feelings and health: 'je me sens mal' = I feel unwell. Without 'se', sentir means to smell or to sense.
Latin mansio 'a stopping place' (same root as English 'mansion'). 'à la maison' = at home; 'fait maison' = homemade.
From Italian appartamento. Spelled with two p's and one t more than English 'apartment'. 'un deux-pièces' = a one-bedroom flat (two rooms).
Latin camera 'vault', which also gave 'camera' and 'chamber'. Only the bedroom: a room in general is 'une pièce'. 'une chambre d'hôtel' = a hotel room.
Latin coquina. Both the room and the cooking: 'la cuisine française'. 'faire la cuisine' = to cook.
Also written salle de bains. It holds the bath or shower, not necessarily a toilet, which is a separate room, 'les toilettes'.
Always plural in French. Asking 'Où sont les toilettes ?' is the normal phrase; 'les WC' ('vé-cé') is also understood.

example.target: Où sont les toilettes, s'il vous plaît ?

note: From Italian salone, a big hall. Also a trade fair ('le Salon de l'auto') and a hairdresser's ('salon de coiffure').
Latin porta. 'la porte d'entrée' = front door. The old city gates of Paris survive as names: Porte de Versailles, Porte Maillot.
Latin fenestra; the circumflex marks the lost s, and English keeps it in 'defenestration'. 'par la fenêtre' = through the window.
Latin lectus. Final t silent: 'lee'. 'aller au lit' = to go to bed; 'un grand lit' = a double bed.
A Parisian variant of chaire (Latin cathedra); chaire survives for a pulpit or a professor's chair. 'une chaise longue' = a deckchair.
From Latin conopeum, a mosquito-netted bed. Also the little toasted snack, canapé, which English borrowed.
Informal short form of 'le réfrigérateur' (or the brand name Frigidaire). 'mettre au frigo' = to put in the fridge.
Also spelled clef; both are pronounced 'klé'. Latin clavis. 'fermer à clé' = to lock; 'un mot-clé' = a keyword.
Usually singular in French where English says 'stairs': 'prendre l'escalier'. 'l'escalier roulant' = escalator.
From Frankish gardo; English 'garden' came via Norman French. 'le jardin public' = the park. 'faire du jardinage' = to garden.
Latin murus. 'le mur du son' = the sound barrier. The adjective is mural, as in English.
Greek lampas via Latin. 'une lampe de poche' = a torch / flashlight, literally a pocket lamp.
Latin furnus (as in 'furnace'). 'un four à micro-ondes' = a microwave. In theatre slang 'un four' is a flop.
The ground floor is 'le rez-de-chaussée'; 'le premier étage' is the first floor above it, like British usage. 'à l'étage' = upstairs.
Silent h: j'habite, with liaison in nous habitons. Used with or without à: 'j'habite (à) Paris'. Latin habitare.
Irregular; past participle vécu ('j'ai vécu à Rome'). Latin vivere. 'Vive la France!' is its subjunctive.
From net 'clean'. The y becomes i before a silent ending: je nettoie, nous nettoyons. 'le nettoyage' = cleaning.
An -ir verb with -er endings in the present; past participle ouvert. 'ouvert' and 'fermé' are the signs on shop doors.
Regular -er verb, from Latin firmare 'to make firm'. 'fermé le lundi' = closed on Mondays. 'Ferme-la!' is rude: shut up.
Latin vestimentum. The circumflex marks the s that English keeps in 'vestment'. Usually plural; 'un vêtement' = one garment.
From Late Latin camisia, the source of English 'chemise' and 'camisole'. Also a folder for papers. 'une chemise à manches courtes' = short-sleeved shirt.
Singular in French: 'un pantalon' = one pair of trousers. Named after Pantalone, the Venetian comedy character in long trousers.
Frankish origin (originally 'plunder, stolen clothes', related to 'rob'). 'une robe de chambre' = a dressing gown.
From Arabic jubba via Italian giubba. 'une mini-jupe'; 'une jupe longue' = a long skirt.
Latin mantellum, as in 'mantle'. Plural manteaux. 'un manteau d'hiver' = a winter coat.
False friend: une veste is a jacket, not a vest. A vest/undershirt is 'un maillot de corps', a waistcoat 'un gilet'.
Short for 'pull-over', borrowed from English. Plural pulls. 'un pull en laine' = a wool jumper.
English loan, also written tee-shirt. Pronounced 'tee-sheurt'. Plural: des t-shirts.
From chausser 'to put on footwear', Latin calceus. 'une paire de chaussures'; 'les chaussures de sport' = trainers, also 'les baskets'.
Diminutive of chausse, the old word for hose/stockings. 'une chaussette' = one sock.
From Latin cappellum, 'little cape'; English 'chapel' and 'chaplet' share the root. 'Chapeau!' = hats off, well done.
A long winter scarf. A square silk scarf is 'un foulard'. The mayor's tricolour sash is also 'une écharpe'.
Frankish origin. Final ts silent: 'gan'. 'aller comme un gant' = to fit like a glove. 'une boîte à gants' = glove compartment.
Latin cinctura 'girding'. 'la ceinture de sécurité' = seat belt; 'se serrer la ceinture' = to tighten one's belt.
Latin saccus, ultimately Semitic. 'un sac à main' = a handbag; 'un sac à dos' = a backpack; 'un sac plastique'.
Also means 'waist' and 'height'. 'Quelle taille faites-vous ?' = what size are you? Shoe size is 'la pointure'.

example.en: Do you have the next size up?

note: Regular -er verb, Latin portare. 'Elle porte une robe rouge.' Also 'to carry': 'porter une valise'. 'prêt-à-porter' = ready-to-wear.
Irregular: one t in the singular, two in the plural; past participle mis. 'mettre un manteau' = to put on a coat; also 'to put' in general.

example.target: Mets ton manteau, il fait froid.
example.en: Put your coat on, it's cold.

note: en- + lever (to lift). The e takes a grave accent when the next syllable is silent: j'enlève, nous enlevons. Also 'to remove' or 'to kidnap'.
Reflexive; silent h so the pronoun elides. 'bien habillé(e)' = well dressed. Opposite: se déshabiller.
Diminutive of lune (moon), for the round lenses. Always plural for spectacles; 'une lunette' alone is a telescope. 'les lunettes de soleil' = sunglasses.
Singular in French: 'un jean' = a pair of jeans. 'Jean' comes from Gênes, the French name of Genoa, where the cloth was made; 'denim' is 'de Nîmes'.
From 'Croate': 17th-century Croatian mercenaries in Paris wore knotted neckcloths. English 'cravat' is the same word.
maillot covers any close-fitting top: 'le maillot jaune' of the Tour de France, a football 'maillot'. Pronounced 'ma-yo'.
From Latin tripalium, a three-staked instrument of torture; English 'travel' comes from the same word. Plural travaux (roadworks: 'travaux').
Regular -er verb; -aill- sounds 'eye': 'tra-va-yé'. 'Je travaille chez Renault' = I work at Renault.
Both the room and the desk, from 'bure', the coarse cloth once covering writing tables. Plural bureaux. 'au bureau' = at the office.
Latin schola; the acute accent marks the lost s that English 'school' keeps. 'l'école primaire', then 'le collège' (11-15) and 'le lycée' (15-18).
Casually 'la fac' (faculté). The Sorbonne, founded in the 13th century, is the historic Paris university.
For university students; schoolchildren are 'des élèves'. The feminine sounds the t. 'une carte d'étudiant' = student card.
Used for secondary and university teachers; casually 'le/la prof'. The feminine 'la professeure' is now accepted. A primary teacher is 'un instituteur / une institutrice'.
From élever 'to raise'. Same form for both; only the article changes. 'un bon élève' = a good pupil.
Latin cursus. Final s silent and the spelling never changes: 'un cours', 'des cours'. 'un cours de français'. Homophone of court (short).

example.target: J'ai un cours de français à dix heures.
example.en: I have a French class at ten.

note: Latin liber. 'le livre' (book) is masculine; 'la livre' (pound, weight or sterling) is feminine. 'un livre de poche' = a paperback.
From Latin quaterni, four folded sheets, which also gave 'quire'. Pronounced 'ka-yé'.
Short for stylographe, from Latin stilus. 'un stylo-bille' = a ballpoint; the brand name Bic is used for cheap ones.
Final -en is nasal: 'eg-za-man'. 'passer un examen' means to sit an exam, not to pass it; passing is 'réussir'. 'le bac' is the school-leaving exam.
Conjugated like prendre; past participle appris. 'apprendre à nager' = to learn to swim. Also 'to teach': 'apprendre quelque chose à quelqu'un'.

example.target: J'apprends le français depuis un an.
example.en: I have been learning French for a year.

note: Regular -er verb. 'étudier la médecine' = to study medicine. For doing homework, French says 'travailler' or 'réviser' (to revise).
Irregular; past participle lu. Latin legere. 'il lit' is spelled like 'le lit' (bed). 'la lecture' = reading, not a lecture.
Irregular, with -v- in the plural; past participle écrit. Latin scribere, the acute accent standing in for the lost s. 'un écrivain' = a writer.
Like prendre: com- 'together' + prendre 'take'. 'Je ne comprends pas' is the learner's lifeline. Also 'to include': 'service compris'.

example.target: Je ne comprends pas. Vous pouvez répéter ?
example.en: I don't understand. Can you repeat?

note: From réunir 'to bring together'. 'être en réunion' = to be in a meeting. The island of La Réunion has the same name.
From entreprendre 'to undertake'; English 'enterprise'. 'une petite entreprise'; 'un entrepreneur' is a French word English took whole.
Same form for both; only the article changes. 'un collègue de bureau'. Latin collega 'one chosen together with'.
Latin patronus. Also the owner of a café or shop: 'la patronne' behind the bar. In sewing un patron is a pattern.
Latin salarium, originally the soldiers' salt money (sal). 'le SMIC' is the French minimum wage.
From Latin ministerium 'service'. 'Quel est votre métier ?' = what do you do? Also a weaving loom: 'métier à tisser'.
Latin lingua: both 'tongue' and 'language', as in older English. 'la langue maternelle' = mother tongue; 'le langage' is language as a faculty or style.
One word for both weather and time, from Latin tempus. Final ps silent: 'tan'. 'Quel temps fait-il ?' asks about the weather; 'je n'ai pas le temps' = I have no time.
French weather uses faire (to make): 'il fait beau', 'il fait froid'. Here the t of fait links to il: 'fè-teel'.
The standard good-weather sentence. Opposites: 'il fait mauvais' (bad weather), 'il fait gris' (grey).

example.target: Il fait beau, on va à la plage ?
example.en: The weather's nice, shall we go to the beach?

note: From pleuvoir, used only with il. Past: 'il a plu'; 'il pleut des cordes' = it's raining ropes, i.e. cats and dogs.
From neiger, impersonal like pleuvoir. 'Il a neigé toute la nuit' = it snowed all night.
Latin pluvia. Pronounced 'plwee'. 'sous la pluie' = in the rain; 'un parapluie' is 'against-rain', an umbrella.
Latin nix, nivis. 'un bonhomme de neige' = a snowman; 'des œufs en neige' = whipped egg whites. 'Blanche-Neige' = Snow White.
Latin sol. -eil sounds 'ay': 'so-lay'. 'Il y a du soleil' = it's sunny; 'un coup de soleil' = sunburn. Louis XIV was 'le Roi-Soleil'.
Latin ventus. Final t silent: 'van', a homophone of vingt and vin. 'Il y a du vent' = it's windy; 'dans le vent' = trendy.
Latin nubes. 'un ciel nuageux' = a cloudy sky; 'être dans les nuages' = to have one's head in the clouds. Also 'le cloud' for computing.
Latin caelum. Also 'heaven': the plural cieux is used for heaven, ciels for painted skies. 'bleu ciel' = sky blue.

example.target: Le ciel est gris ce matin.
example.en: The sky is grey this morning.

note: Latin calidus. 'Il fait chaud' = it's hot (weather), but 'j'ai chaud' = I'm hot: French uses avoir for feeling hot or cold. The d is silent in chaud.
Latin frigidus. 'Il fait froid' / 'j'ai froid'. Pronounced 'frwa', d silent in the masculine. 'le froid' = the cold.
Latin mare. Sounds exactly like mère (mother) and maire (mayor). 'au bord de la mer' = at the seaside; 'la Méditerranée' is 'the sea in the middle of lands'.
From Latin montanea. -gne sounds 'ny': 'mon-tany'. 'à la montagne' = in the mountains; 'le Mont Blanc' is Western Europe's highest.
From Italian piaggia. 'à la plage' = at the beach; 'une serviette de plage' = a beach towel.
The circumflex marks the s of Old French forest, which English kept. 'la forêt de Fontainebleau'. Final t silent.
A river that flows into another river; a river reaching the sea is 'un fleuve' (la Seine, la Loire are fleuves). English 'river' is the same word.
Latin arbor. Masculine despite ending in -e. 'un arbre fruitier' = a fruit tree; 'l'arbre de Noël' = Christmas tree.
Latin flos, floris. 'la fleur de lis' was the royal emblem; 'fleurir' = to bloom; 'un bouquet de fleurs'.
Latin canis; the feminine 'la chienne' is a female dog. 'Attention, chien méchant' = beware of the dog. Nasal -ien: 'shyan'.
Late Latin cattus. The t is silent: 'sha'; 'la chatte' is the female. 'avoir un chat dans la gorge' = to have a frog in one's throat.
Pronounced 'wa-zo': none of its letters sounds as written. Plural oiseaux. From Latin avicellus, a little bird (avis).
Latin luna. 'la pleine lune' = full moon; 'être dans la lune' = to be daydreaming; 'la lune de miel' = honeymoon.
Latin stella; the acute é replaces the lost s (Old French estoile). 'une étoile filante' = a shooting star; 'un hôtel trois étoiles'.
Literally 'silver' (Latin argentum), as silver coins were money; chemical symbol Ag. 'l'argent de poche' = pocket money. Final t silent.

example.target: Je n'ai pas d'argent sur moi.
example.en: I don't have any money on me.

note: Latin pretium. Final x silent: 'pree'. Also 'prize': 'le prix Goncourt', 'le prix Nobel'. 'à tout prix' = at any price.
'C'est trop cher' = it's too expensive. Also 'dear' in letters: 'Cher Paul, Chère Marie'. 'coûter cher' uses the invariable adverb.
Invariable: 'des chaussures bon marché'. In speech 'pas cher' is far more common. Le Bon Marché is a famous Paris department store.
From Arabic makhazin 'storehouses' via Italian; English 'magazine' began with the same meaning. 'un grand magasin' = a department store.
Latin mercatus. Open-air food markets are a weekly fixture in every French town. 'faire le marché' = to shop at the market.

example.target: Le marché a lieu le samedi matin.
example.en: The market takes place on Saturday mornings.

note: Chains: Carrefour, Leclerc, Intermarché. A very large one is 'un hypermarché'. 'faire les courses' = to do the shopping.
From boulanger (baker), originally a maker of round loaves (boules). Also sells pastries if it is a 'boulangerie-pâtisserie'.
Classic false friend: a librairie sells books; a library is 'une bibliothèque'. Latin librarius 'of books'.
Literally a box or crate (Latin capsa). 'passer à la caisse' = to go to the checkout; 'le caissier / la caissière' = cashier.
Often 'la carte bleue' or 'la CB', after the original French debit card scheme. 'payer par carte' = to pay by card; 'sans contact' = contactless.
From Latin species. 'Vous payez en espèces ou par carte ?' Informally 'en liquide' (in liquid) or 'du cash'.

example.target: Vous payez en espèces ou par carte ?
example.en: Are you paying in cash or by card?

note: France's currency since 2002, replacing the franc. Takes a plural s: 'dix euros', with a z liaison: 'dee-zeu-ro'.
The e takes a grave accent when the following ending is silent: j'achète, but nous achetons. 'faire des achats' = to go shopping.
Regular -re verb, Latin vendere. 'à vendre' = for sale; 'un vendeur / une vendeuse' = shop assistant.
Both je paie and je paye are accepted. From Latin pacare 'to appease'. 'payer par carte', 'c'est moi qui paie' = it's on me.
The circumflex marks the s of Old French couster (Latin constare). 'Ça coûte combien ?' = how much does it cost? 'coûter cher' = to be expensive.
Everyday form; more formal: 'Ça fait combien ?' or 'Combien ça coûte ?'. combien = com(me) + bien, 'how well/much'.

example.target: C'est combien, le kilo de tomates ?
example.en: How much is a kilo of tomatoes?

note: False friend: monnaie is small change or currency, not money in general (that is l'argent). From Juno Moneta, whose Roman temple housed the mint. 'Gardez la monnaie' = keep the change.
ticket itself came back from English, which had taken it from French 'étiquette'. A formal receipt or bill is 'le reçu' or 'la facture'.
Latin gratuitus. Free as in 'no cost'; free as in 'liberty' is libre. 'entrée gratuite' = free admission. The t is heard only in the feminine.
Always plural for the sales season; France holds two legally regulated sales periods a year, in January and in summer. 'en solde' = reduced.
'une paire de chaussures', 'une paire de lunettes'. Homophones: père (father) and pair (even number).
'une pièce de deux euros'. The same word means a room, a part, a play ('une pièce de théâtre') and a document ('pièce d'identité').
A round trip: Old French bougette 'little bag' went to England, became 'budget' for the Chancellor's bag of accounts, and came back to French in the 18th century.
From heur 'luck' (Latin augurium), so 'lucky' at root; 'bonheur' and 'malheur' are good and bad luck. Silent h; -eux silent, -euse sounds the z.

example.target: Je suis très heureuse de vous voir.
example.en: I'm very happy to see you.

note: Latin tristis. Same form m/f. 'C'est triste' = that's sad; 'la tristesse' = sadness.
'Je suis content(e)' is the everyday 'I'm happy / glad'. False friend only in part: it does not mean 'content' as in satisfied-and-calm.
Past participle of fatiguer, Latin fatigare. 'Je suis fatigué(e)'; 'la fatigue' passed into English unchanged.

example.target: Je suis fatigué, je vais me coucher.
example.en: I'm tired, I'm going to bed.

note: From Latin cholera, the bile that was thought to cause anger. 'Il est en colère contre moi' = he is angry with me. Also fâché(e).
Fear, hunger, thirst, heat and cold are things you 'have' in French. 'J'ai peur des chiens' = I'm afraid of dogs. 'N'ayez pas peur!' = don't be afraid.
Never 'je suis faim'. Latin fames. 'J'ai très faim' = I'm very hungry; 'j'ai une faim de loup' = I could eat a horse.

example.en: Are you hungry? Shall we eat?

note: Latin sitis. 'J'ai soif' = I'm thirsty. The f is pronounced.
Latin amare. 'Je t'aime' = I love you, but 'j'aime bien Paul' is only 'I like Paul': adding bien weakens it. For things, aimer = to like.
Regular -er. Stronger than aimer for things and hobbies: 'J'adore le chocolat'. Also to worship.
Regular -er, Latin detestari. 'Je déteste attendre' = I hate waiting. 'détestable' is the adjective.
The second accent turns grave when the ending is silent: je préfère, nous préférons. 'Je préfère le thé au café' = I prefer tea to coffee.
Latin amor. Masculine in the singular; in literary style the plural 'les amours' is feminine. 'un coup de foudre' = love at first sight (a thunderbolt).
Latin gaudia. Pronounced 'zhwa'. 'la joie de vivre' is used in English too; 'avec joie' = gladly.
Past participle of surprendre. The masculine s is silent; the feminine surprise is also the noun 'une surprise'.
in- + quiet, 'not quiet'. 'Ne t'inquiète pas' = don't worry. The t is silent in inquiet, heard in inquiète.

example.target: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout va bien.

note: From nerf (nerve). Means jumpy or highly strung; for exam nerves, 'stressé(e)' is more common.
Same form m/f. From Italian calma, ultimately Greek kauma 'the heat of the day', when the wind drops. 'Du calme!' = calm down.
Latin ferus 'wild', softened to 'proud'. 'fier de' = proud of: 'Je suis fière de toi.' Pronounced 'fyèr' in both genders.
Greek zelos via Latin; English 'jealous' and 'zealous' are its two descendants. -oux silent, -ouse with a z.
'être amoureux de' = to be in love with. 'tomber amoureux' = to fall in love. Also a noun: 'les amoureux' = lovers, sweethearts.

example.target: Il est amoureux de sa voisine.
example.en: He is in love with his neighbour.

note: Irregular; past participle ri. Latin ridere. 'rire de' = to laugh at; 'sourire' (to smile) is 'under-laugh'. 'le rire' = laughter.
Regular -er, Latin plorare. 'pleurer de joie' = to cry with joy. 'les larmes' = tears.
bon + heur (luck, Latin augurium): happiness was good fortune. Opposite: le malheur. 'par bonheur' = luckily.
Latin solus. 'tout seul' = all alone; before a noun it means 'only': 'le seul problème' = the only problem.

en: to go home, to come back
note: re- + entrer. Takes être in the past: 'je suis rentré(e) tard'. 'rentrer à la maison' = to go home; 'la rentrée' is the September return to school and work.
Latin habere. The main auxiliary of the past tense: 'j'ai mangé'. Also for age and feelings: 'j'ai trente ans', 'j'ai froid'. Past participle eu, pronounced 'u'.
Irregular; 'nous faisons' is pronounced 'feu-zon'; 'vous faites' is one of only three -tes forms (with êtes, dites). Past participle fait. Weather and sport use faire.

example.target: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
example.en: What are you doing this weekend?

note: Built from three Latin verbs: ire (irai), vadere (vais, va) and ambulare (allons). Takes être in the past: 'je suis allé(e)'. 'aller + infinitive' = going to.

example.target: On va au cinéma ce soir ?
example.en: Shall we go to the cinema tonight?

note: Irregular; past participle venu with être. 'venir de + infinitive' = to have just done: 'je viens de manger' = I've just eaten.
Irregular; past participle pu. In questions 'Puis-je' replaces 'peux-je'. 'Vous pouvez répéter ?' = could you repeat? 'le pouvoir' = power.
Irregular; past participle voulu. 'Je veux' is blunt; 'je voudrais' is polite. 'vouloir dire' = to mean: 'Ça veut dire quoi ?'.
Irregular; past participle dû keeps a circumflex to differ from du. Also 'to owe': 'Tu me dois dix euros'. 'le devoir' = duty; 'les devoirs' = homework.
Knowing facts and skills: 'je sais nager' = I can swim. Past participle su. 'Je ne sais pas' is often slurred to 'chais pas'. Compare connaître.
'vous dites', not 'disez'. Past participle dit. Latin dicere. 'Comment dit-on ... en français ?' = how do you say ... in French?

example.target: Comment dit-on « thank you » en français ?
example.en: How do you say 'thank you' in French?

note: Regular -er, the model verb of the first group. 'parler français' with no article; 'parler à quelqu'un' = to talk to someone. 'le parlement' is where people talk.
Irregular, -y- in nous/vous; past participle vu. Latin videre. 'On verra' = we'll see; 'Voyons!' = come on now.
Regular -er, Latin donare. 'donner sur' = to look out onto (a room 'gives onto' the sea). 'Donnez-moi ...' = give me.
Reflexive; grave accent appears before silent endings (je me lève / nous nous levons). Without se: lever = to raise. 'Le soleil se lève' = the sun rises.

example.target: Je me lève à sept heures.

note: Reflexive, Latin lavare. With a body part the pronoun stays and the article replaces 'my': 'je me lave les mains'. 'le lave-linge' = washing machine.
Latin circare 'to go around'; English 'search' came from it via Old French cerchier. No preposition: 'je cherche la gare'. 'aller chercher' = to fetch.
Regular -er; the troubadours were 'finders' of songs. Also 'to think': 'Je trouve ça cher' = I find that expensive. 'se trouver' = to be located.
Regular -er; no preposition: 'regarder la télé'. False friend: it is not 'regard'. 'Regarde!' = look!

example.target: On regarde un film ce soir ?
example.en: Shall we watch a film tonight?

note: Latin auscultare (as in 'auscultation'). No preposition: 'écouter la radio'. 'Écoutez...' opens many French sentences, like 'look...' in English.
The model regular -ir verb (second group), with -iss- in the plural. Past participle fini. 'C'est fini' = it's over.
Regular -er; nous commençons takes a cedilla to keep the soft c. 'commencer à + infinitive' = to begin to. 'le commencement' = the beginning.
Latin pensare 'to weigh'; peser (to weigh) is its twin. 'penser à' = to think about; 'penser que' = to think that. 'Je pense, donc je suis' (Descartes).
Familiarity with people and places: 'je connais Paris', 'tu connais Marie ?'. The circumflex sits on î before t (il connaît); past participle connu. Facts use savoir.

example.target: Vous connaissez un bon restaurant ici ?
example.en: Do you know a good restaurant here?

note: Irregular -ir verb like partir and dormir; être in the past ('je suis sorti'). 'sortir avec quelqu'un' = to date someone. 'la sortie' = exit.
Also 'to work' for machines: 'ça marche' = it works / OK, deal. Frankish origin, related to 'march'. 'faire une marche' = to go for a hike.
Latin qui. Never elided: 'Qui est-ce ?' = who is it? 'Qui est là ?' Also the relative 'who/which' as subject: 'l'homme qui parle'.
Elides to qu' before a vowel: 'Qu'est-ce que c'est ?' = what is it? At the end of a sentence it becomes quoi: 'Tu fais quoi ?'.
The grave accent exists only to tell où (where) from ou (or); it is the only French word with ù. 'Où est la gare ?' 'D'où venez-vous ?' = where are you from?
Latin quando. The d is silent, but links as t before a vowel: 'quand est-ce' sounds 'kan-tès'. 'Quand ?' = when?; as a conjunction: 'quand je serai grand'.
pour + quoi. The answer begins with parce que. 'Pourquoi pas ?' = why not?
'Comment ça va ?', 'Comment vous appelez-vous ?'. On its own, 'Comment ?' is a polite 'pardon?'. Final t silent except in liaison.
com(me) + bien. 'Combien de personnes ?' = how many people? 'C'est combien ?' = how much is it? 'le combien' asks the date informally.
Agrees with its noun: quel jour, quelle heure, quels livres, quelles chaussures. All four sound the same: 'kel'. Also an exclamation: 'Quelle belle maison!'.
The t is never pronounced and never linked: 'et un' is 'é un'. Pronounced like é. Do not confuse with 'est' (is).
No accent: ou = or, où = where. 'ou bien' = or else. 'thé ou café ?'.
Latin magis 'more'. Final s silent: 'mè'. 'Mais oui!' = yes of course; 'mais non!' = of course not.
par + ce + que. Becomes 'parce qu'' before a vowel: 'parce qu'il pleut'. The answer to pourquoi. 'à cause de' = because of (+ noun).
Latin apud hoc. The final c is pronounced: 'a-vek'. 'avec plaisir' = with pleasure; 'Tu viens avec ?' (coming along?) is casual.
Latin sine. Final s silent except in liaison: 'sans argent' = 'san-zar-jan'. 'sans doute' means 'probably', not 'without doubt'.
Latin pro. 'pour moi' = for me; 'pour + infinitive' = in order to: 'pour aller à la gare'. 'le pour et le contre' = the pros and cons.
'dans la maison' = in the house; 'dans dix minutes' = in ten minutes' time. For cities and countries use à / en instead: à Paris, en France.
Latin super. 'sur la table'. Also 'out of': 'dix sur vingt' = ten out of twenty. Sounds like sûr (sure), which has a circumflex.
Latin trans 'beyond'. Silent s except in liaison: 'très important' = 'trè-zam-por-tan'. 'très bien' = very good.
'Moi aussi' = me too. In a comparison, 'aussi ... que' = as ... as. For 'neither / me neither' use 'non plus': 'moi non plus'.
pas was once 'a step' ('I don't walk a step'); it became the real negative, and spoken French now often drops ne: 'je sais pas'. ne becomes n' before a vowel.
beau + coup. 'beaucoup de' before a noun with no article: 'beaucoup de monde' = lots of people. Never 'très beaucoup'.
'par ici' = this way; 'ici' on the phone: 'Ici Marie' = Marie speaking. Opposite: là-bas (over there).
For friends, family, children, students among themselves and online. Using tu with a stranger can offend; the verb for switching is 'tutoyer'. Elides only in slang: 't'es'.
Polite singular and any plural. Shopkeepers, officials and strangers get vous; 'On peut se tutoyer ?' asks to switch. The s links before a vowel: 'vous êtes' = 'vou-zèt'.
From homme (Latin homo). Takes a singular verb but in speech it replaces nous: 'On y va ?' = shall we go? Also 'one / they': 'on parle français ici'.
Latin grandis. Goes before the noun: 'une grande maison'. For people it means tall. The d is silent in grand but links as t: 'un grand ami' = 'gran-ta-mi'.
Before the noun: 'un petit café'. Silent t in petit, heard in petite. 'le petit déjeuner', 'petit à petit' = little by little.
Latin bonus. Before the noun: 'un bon vin'. The masculine n is nasal; bonne sounds the n. 'bon' alone also means 'right then' or 'OK'.
Before the noun: 'un mauvais film'. 'Il fait mauvais' = the weather is bad. Silent s in the masculine, z sound in mauvaise.
Three forms: beau, belle, and bel before a masculine noun starting with a vowel: 'un bel homme'. Plural beaux. 'beau-père' is a father-in-law or stepfather.
Possibly from Old Norse jol, the Yule feast, i.e. 'festive'. Before the noun: 'une jolie robe'. English 'jolly' is the same word.
Like beau: nouveau, nouvelle, and nouvel before a vowel ('le nouvel an' = New Year). 'nouveau' = new to you; 'neuf' = brand new.
Three forms: vieux, vieille, and vieil before a vowel ('un vieil homme'). Before the noun. 'mon vieux' = old chap, mate.
Latin juvenis. Same form m/f; before the noun: 'un jeune homme', 'une jeune femme'. 'les jeunes' = young people.
Before the noun: 'un gros chien'. For people it means fat, so use grand for tall. 'un gros problème' = a big problem; 'gros bisous' = big kisses.
Latin longus. The g is silent in long and the feminine adds -ue to keep a hard g. 'le long de' = along.
Latin curtus. Sounds like cours (class) and cour (courtyard) in the masculine. 'à court de' = short of; 'un court-métrage' = a short film.
Latin facilis, from facere 'to do'. Same form m/f. 'C'est facile!' English 'facile' survives with a negative sense.

example.target: Le français n'est pas si facile.

note: Same form m/f. 'C'est difficile à dire' = it's hard to say. Also 'fussy': 'un enfant difficile'.
Same form m/f. 'un train rapide'. The adverb is vite: 'Vite!' = quick! 'rapidement' also exists.
Latin lentus. Silent t in lent, heard in lente. Adverb: lentement. 'au ralenti' = in slow motion.
Latin fortis. Also 'loud' (parler fort) and as an adverb 'very' in formal French. 'un café fort' = strong coffee; 'c'est pas mon fort' = not my strong point.
Latin flebilis 'to be wept over'; English 'feeble' is the same word. Same form m/f. 'un point faible' = a weak point.
Before the noun it means 'own': 'ma propre voiture' = my own car; after it, 'clean': 'une voiture propre'. Latin proprius.
Frankish origin, related to English 'sallow'. Same form m/f. 'les mains sales'. Before a noun it is an insult: 'sale type' = nasty guy.
Also 'good value': 'un prix intéressant' = an attractive price. Double s, unlike English 'interesting'.
From ennui, which English borrowed. Also 'annoying': 'c'est ennuyeux' can mean 'that's a nuisance'. Informal: 'chiant' (vulgar), 'nul' (rubbish).
Latin gentilis 'of good family', as in English 'gentle' and 'genteel'. The l is silent in gentil ('jan-tee'); gentille sounds 'jan-tee-y'. 'C'est gentil' = that's kind.
Also 'large' in amount: 'une somme importante' = a large sum. 'C'est important' = it matters.
Classic false friend: sensible means sensitive ('une peau sensible'), not sensible. For 'sensible' say raisonnable or sensé. Same form m/f.
Latin villa, a country estate, which grew into a town. The ll is an l here: 'veel'. 'en ville' = in town, downtown; 'une grande ville' = a city.
From Latin villaticum, the estate's hamlet. English took the word from French. 'un petit village' is the archetype of rural France.
Latin ruga 'wrinkle, furrow'. Street names put rue first: 'rue de Rivoli'. 'dans la rue', not 'sur': 'il habite dans la rue Pasteur'.

example.en: I live on Victor Hugo Street.

note: A town square: 'la place de la Bastille'. Also a seat or a parking space ('une place de parking') and room ('il n'y a pas de place').
Pronounced 'santr-veel'. Signs read 'Centre-ville'. 'au centre-ville' = downtown. 'la vieille ville' = the old town.
Greek ekklesia 'assembly' via Latin. A cathedral is 'la cathédrale'; 'Notre-Dame' is 'Our Lady'. 'l'Église' with a capital is the institution.
Latin museum, the seat of the Muses. Masculine despite the -ée ending (like lycée). 'le musée du Louvre'; national museums are free on the first Sunday of the month.
Final c pronounced: 'park'. 'le parc d'attractions' = theme park. The gardens of Paris are called 'jardins' (jardin du Luxembourg) as often as parcs.
Latin pons, pontis. Final t silent: 'pon'. 'le Pont-Neuf' (new bridge) is the oldest bridge in Paris. 'faire le pont' = to take a long weekend.
From Italian banca, the money-changer's bench. 'un compte en banque' = a bank account; 'la Banque de France'. 'une banque' is also a database or blood bank.
'la poste' (f.) is the post office and the mail; 'le poste' (m.) is a job, a radio set or an extension number. 'un timbre' = a stamp.
From maire (mayor). Big cities say 'l'hôtel de ville'. Civil weddings must take place there, before any church wedding.

example.target: La mairie est sur la place principale.
example.en: The town hall is on the main square.

note: Short for cinématographe, the Lumière brothers' 1895 invention from Greek kinema 'movement'. Casually 'le ciné'. 'une séance' = a screening.
Greek theatron 'viewing place'. The circumflex on â is simply traditional here. 'une pièce de théâtre' = a play.
Greek biblion 'book' + theke 'case'. Not to be confused with librairie (a bookshop). Also a bookcase at home.
From bâtir 'to build'; the circumflex marks the s of Old French bastir. 'le bâtiment' is also the building trade. A block of flats is 'un immeuble'.
'la tour' (f.) is a tower, 'la tour Eiffel'; 'le tour' (m.) is a turn or a tour, 'le Tour de France'. Latin turris.
Latin castellum; the circumflex marks the s of Old French chastel, which English kept in 'castle'. Plural châteaux. Also a wine estate: 'Château Margaux'.
Originally a quarter of a town. 'le Quartier latin' is the Paris student district, named for the Latin once spoken at the Sorbonne. 'un commerçant de quartier' = a local shopkeeper.
Latin piscina, a fish pond. 'la piscine municipale' = the public pool, where a swimming cap is often compulsory.
Greek stadion, a race length. 'le Stade de France' is the national stadium in Saint-Denis. Also 'stage' of a process: 'à ce stade'.
Latin cuneus 'wedge'. 'au coin de la rue' = on the street corner; 'le café du coin' = the local café; 'dans le coin' = around here.

example.target: Il y a une pharmacie au coin de la rue.
example.en: There is a pharmacy on the corner of the street.

note: Regular -er. Only for places: 'visiter un musée'. Visiting a person is 'rendre visite à' or 'aller voir'. 'une visite guidée' = a guided tour.

example.target: Nous allons visiter le château demain.
example.en: We are going to visit the castle tomorrow.

note: Latin pagus 'district'. Pronounced 'pé-ee', with the s silent. 'le pays' also means home region: 'le vin du pays' = local wine. 'les Pays-Bas' = the Netherlands.
Latin caput 'head'. Feminine for the city ('Paris est la capitale'); 'le capital' is money capital, and 'une capitale' is also a capital letter.
